title: Grade 1 Maths Homework: A Calm Parent's Guide (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Grade 1 Maths Homework: A Parent's Guide + Quiz
meta_desc: Help with Grade 1 maths homework without doing it for your child: what it covers, a calm 10-minute routine, concrete-first tricks, and a free quiz.
excerpt: Grade 1 maths homework looks easy to adults — which is exactly why so many of us get it wrong. Here is how to help a six-year-old without taking the pencil, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
The homework sheet says ‘draw 7 balloons and colour 4’, and your Class 1 child has drawn nine, coloured six, and is now cheerfully colouring the table. To you this is trivial. To a six-year-old it is three separate jobs — count out seven, stop, then colour exactly four — and holding all three in mind at once is the actual lesson. That gap, between how easy Grade 1 maths homework looks to us and how much is really going on for the child, is where most homework friction begins.

The good news: Grade 1 maths homework is genuinely low-stakes, and ten calm minutes a day is plenty. The catch is that the adult habits that feel helpful — correcting fast, showing the answer, pushing for speed — are the ones that quietly do the most harm at this age. This guide covers what Class 1 homework contains, how to help without hijacking it, a calm routine, quick wins per topic, and when to ask the teacher.

What Grade 1 maths homework actually covers

The NCERT-aligned Class 1 course (the new Joyful Mathematics books) is deliberately gentle and hands-on. Homework at this level is less about right answers and more about building number sense. Across the year expect sheets on:

  • Counting and writing numbers to 100 — saying them in order, and matching the number to the right quantity of objects.
  • Addition and subtraction within 20 — joining groups and taking away, mostly with pictures and counters rather than bare sums.
  • Number bonds and one more / one less — the pairs that make 10, and knowing the number just before and after.
  • Shapes and patterns — circles, squares, triangles, and copying or extending a colour or shape pattern.
  • Comparing and simple measurement — bigger and smaller, longer and shorter, heavier and lighter, and telling day from night.

Notice what is not here: no carrying, no times tables, no long word problems. Those arrive in Class 2. Grade 1 homework that suddenly demands them is either optional stretch work or a sheet worth querying with the teacher.

How to help without doing it for them

The single rule I give every Class 1 parent: your pencil never touches the sheet. The instant you write the answer, the thinking transfers to you. Your job is to talk, point, and wait.

Concrete, then pictorial, then abstract

This is the one idea that fixes more Grade 1 homework than anything else. If ‘5 + 3’ on paper draws a blank, do not re-explain the digits. Go backwards. First make it concrete — put out five buttons, then three more, and count. Then pictorial — draw five dots and three dots. Only then return to the abstract figures 5 + 3 = 8. A child who has physically pushed eight buttons together understands the sum in a way no explanation of the numerals can deliver. Teachers call this the concrete-pictorial-abstract approach, and at this age you skip the first step at your peril.

Ask, do not tell

When an answer is wrong, swallow the urge to say ‘no, it’s 8’. Ask instead: ‘show me with your buttons?’ or ‘how many did you start with?’ A question hands the thinking back; telling shuts it down. It is slower, and on a tired Tuesday evening that slowness is maddening — but the slowness is the point.

Let the mistake happen

Watching a six-year-old miscount and not jumping in is genuinely hard. Do it anyway. A wrong answer they notice and fix themselves teaches more than a right one you supplied, so give it a beat before you step in.

A calm 10 to 15 minute routine

Grade 1 maths homework should take about ten to fifteen minutes, full stop. If it regularly runs longer or ends in tears, the problem is almost never the child — it is the setup. A pattern that works for the parents I know:

StepWhat to doWhy it helps
Snack and move firstNever straight off the school bus — food, a run around, then sitA hungry, fidgety six-year-old cannot count; ten fed minutes beat thirty tired ones
Keep counters handyA bowl of buttons, beans or coins on the tableTurns any stuck sum into something the child can build with their hands
Read it aloud togetherSay the instruction once, then let them startMost Grade 1 ‘wrong’ answers are misheard or half-read instructions
Stop at fifteen minutesEnd on time even if unfinished, and tell the teacherProtects how your child feels about maths; the teacher needs to know it ran long

Quick wins for the hard bits

Three small habits clear up most Class 1 homework wobbles.

Counting: start from the bigger number

For 2 + 6, most children count out two, then six, then start again from one. Teach them to hold the bigger number, 6, in their head and count on: ‘six … seven, eight.’ Two hops instead of eight. Children find it genuinely delightful once they spot that 2 + 6 and 6 + 2 land in the same place.

Number bonds: fill a ten-frame

The pairs that make ten — 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5 — are the most valuable thing in the whole Grade 1 year. Draw two rows of five squares, drop in some counters, and ask ‘how many more to fill it?’ every day for a fortnight. A child who instantly knows the bonds to ten finds the next four years of arithmetic easier.

Shapes and patterns: say it out loud

For a pattern like red, blue, red, blue, get your child to chant it — the ear catches the rhythm before the eye does, and then the next colour is obvious. For shapes, hunt real ones: the roti is a circle, the window is a square, the samosa is a triangle. Naming shapes around the house sticks far better than the worksheet alone.

When to actually worry

Most Grade 1 stumbles are just part of being six. A few are worth a quiet word with the teacher:

  • Homework consistently takes far longer than fifteen minutes despite a calm setup.
  • By the second half of the year your child still cannot reliably count out ten objects one-to-one.
  • Numbers come out reversed most of the time — writing 6 as an upside-down shape, or reading 12 as 21 — not just occasionally.
  • Real distress around maths specifically: tears, or ‘I can’t do it’ before even trying.

None of these spell trouble. They simply mean your child needs a different kind of practice now rather than later. Grade 1 gaps are cheap to close and expensive to ignore, so flag them early.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Maths Homework Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions covering counting on, number bonds, one more and one less, and shapes. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 maths: counting, number bonds, one more/less and shapes

questions.explanation: Start from the bigger number, 6, and count on two: 7, 8. The answer is 8.
4 and 6 fill a ten-frame exactly. The bonds to ten are 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5.
One more than a number is the very next number. After 9 comes 10.
One less than 15 is 14, which is the number just before it.
Take four away from ten. Using the bond, 4 and 6 make 10, so 10 − 4 = 6.

questions.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
questions.explanation: A triangle has three straight sides and three corners.
This is a double and a bond to ten: 5 and 5 make 10.

questions.q: Rahul has 7 marbles and finds 3 more. How many does he have now?
questions.explanation: This is a joining story: 7 + 3. The bond 7 and 3 makes 10, so he has 10 marbles.

faq.q: How long should Grade 1 maths homework take?
faq.a: About ten to fifteen minutes. If it regularly runs longer despite a calm setup, the sheet is too hard or the idea has not landed yet — stop, note it, and tell the teacher rather than pushing your child through half an hour of frustration.

faq.q: My child still counts on fingers. Is that a problem?
faq.a: Not at all in Grade 1 — fingers make the maths concrete and every six-year-old starts there. The aim is to give better tools, like the number bonds to ten, so they gradually choose to leave fingers behind. Do not ban them.

faq.q: What is the single most useful thing to practise in Grade 1?
faq.a: The number bonds to ten — the pairs 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5. A child who knows these instantly finds addition, subtraction and place value far easier for years afterwards. A daily ten-frame drill is time very well spent.

faq.q: Should I correct every mistake straight away?
faq.a: No. Let your child finish, then look at it together and ask ‘show me with your buttons?’ instead of giving the answer. A mistake a child spots and fixes themselves teaches far more than one you correct for them.
